newsitem.title: USA: Tyson denies wrongdoing in Espy case.
newsitem.headline: Tyson denies wrongdoing in Espy case.

text.p: Poultry processing giant Tyson Foods Inc on Tuesday denied any wrongdoing in its dealings with former U.S. Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy and said charges against Tyson lobbyist Jack Williams were without merit.

"As we have said repeatedly over the past two and one-half years, all of Tyson Foods' dealings with the USDA during Secretary Espy's tenure, as well as throughout the history of the company, have been honest, above board and appropriate," Springdale, Arkansas-based Tyson said in a statement.
"We have never sought or received preferental treatment of any kind from the USDA or any other government agency."

Earlier on Tuesday a federal grand jury indicted Williams, a Washington lobbyist for Tyson, alleging that he lied to the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Agriculture Department's Office of the Inspector General in the preliminary investigation of Espy.
Espy resigned in 1994 amid a swirl of accusations that he broke federal laws by accepting gifts and favors from Tyson and other concerns with business pending before the Agriculture Department.
The indictment was the fifth to be returned in the government's two-year probe of Espy, being conducted by Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz.
"We believe the charges being brought today against Jack Williams have no merit," the Tyson statement said.
"The indictment of Jack Williams by the independent counsel was a complete surprise to Tyson officials and did not follow the usual notification procedures," Tyson said.
"Since neither Mr Williams nor anyone at Tyson Foods is guilty of illegal activity in any of our dealings with the USDA or Secretary Espy, we are confident he will be exonerated," the statement said.
Williams's attorney Henry Schuelke said his client denied all the charges, would fight the indictment and would not agree to any out-of-court settlement with the government.
"Once the jury's heard the entire case, he fully expects to be vindicated," Schuelke said.
